guidance: Use at least three biological replicates per group for any statistical inference; more replicates are needed for small fold changes.
About 5 million mapped reads can quantify medium-to-high expressed genes; up to 100 million reads are used to quantify low-expressed genes and transcripts precisely.
Power to detect DE rises much more with replicates than with depth at moderate depth: at 30M reads, a 1.5-fold change has ~43%/64%/91% power with 3/5/10 replicates; a 2-fold change ~87%/98%/100%.
applies_to: human whole blood, 30M reads, gene with ~70 reads

guidance: Beyond some sequencing depth, adding replicates improves power more than adding reads; tools like Scotty estimate the trade-off under a budget.
Randomize samples across library-preparation batches and sequencing lanes so technical factors are not confounded with the experimental factor.

TPM is more comparable between samples than RPKM/FPKM but still biased by composition; between-sample methods such as TMM correct this. Gene-length correction is not needed when comparing the same gene across samples.
Count-based tools like edgeR take raw counts and handle normalization inside the model; other methods require pre-normalized input.
If condition effects exist, biological replicates of the same condition should cluster together in PCA; check this before DE.
Check quantifications for GC-content and gene-length biases and apply correcting normalization if present (e.g. EDASeq).
SAMseq needs roughly 10 or more replicates for acceptable sensitivity; NOISeq/NOISeqBIO trade some sensitivity for fewer false positives across replicate numbers.
Negative-binomial parametric tools (edgeR, DESeq2) are typically preferred for count data that fit the NB distribution; DESeq2 is among the most widely used and validated.
source: Rosati et al. 2024, Comput Struct Biotechnol J

guidance: Published studies commonly call DEGs at Benjamini-Hochberg FDR < 0.05 with |log2FC| > 1, but cut-offs vary widely (|log2FC| 1.5 or 4, raw P < 0.01). BH-FDR is less conservative than Bonferroni.
source: Rosati et al. 2024, Comput Struct Biotechnol J

guidance: Barcoding can pool up to ~96 samples per lane, trading lower depth per sample for more samples.
Populations of roughly 100-500 individuals are recommended for GWAS in maize; larger and more diverse populations increase discoveries.
source: Sahito et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: When genotypes are tested across locations or years, compute BLUPs or BLUEs to combine environments before GWAS; G×E otherwise reduces heritability.
source: Sahito et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Remove outliers and noisy phenotype records before GWAS, and prefer traits with moderate-to-high heritability.
source: Sahito et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Population structure must be controlled; PCA estimates structure efficiently and is often faster than STRUCTURE.
source: Sahito et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Estimate LD before GWAS. Maize LD decays fast, so more markers are needed; selfing crops have more extensive LD and need fewer markers.
source: Sahito et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Mixed linear models (MLM) are the standard; standard MLM is slow for large datasets, and multi-locus models exist. Studies often compare GLM, MLM and FarmCPU side by side (e.g. in GAPIT).
source: Sahito et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Validate GWAS hits in independent samples and under field conditions; stringent multiple-testing thresholds can miss real associations.
source: Sahito et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: The review states that r^2 below 0.2 indicates co-inheritance. This is backwards: low r^2 means weak LD (alleles NOT inherited together). Do not use this statement.
source: Sahito et al. 2024, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Human GWAS use P < 5×10^-8 for discovery; replication of selected SNPs in an independent sample may use P < 0.05.
After genotyping QC, imputation typically expands array data from about 5 to 15 million variants.
SNP heritability from GWAS is often far below twin estimates (e.g. resting heart rate ~20% vs 55-70%); expect GWAS hits to explain a small share of heritability.
For polygenic scores, the discovery sample must be independent of, similar to, and much larger than the target sample.
Human complex traits can need very large samples; some required millions of individuals to saturate SNP heritability.
A cotton study found multi-locus GWAS methods had better power and accuracy than single-locus MLM (TASSEL).
source: Altaf et al. 2024, Turkish J Botany

guidance: GWAS needs large samples for small effects, control of population stratification to avoid spurious hits, and high-quality dense genotypes.
source: Altaf et al. 2024, Turkish J Botany

guidance: Significance is commonly set at alpha = 0.05 corrected by FDR or Bonferroni; FDR control improves with larger sample size.
source: Yáñez et al. 2023, Reviews in Aquaculture

guidance: One cattle fertility GWAS declared markers significant at a 20% FDR — far more lenient than typical; treat such hits as suggestive.
flag: Example of lenient threshold; useful as a contrast in guided questions

guidance: Bayes C analysis on 1-Mb SNP windows (~21 SNPs per window) is used in livestock GWAS.
GWAS power for disease resistance suffers when few individuals are diseased (e.g. 4% cases) or LD between markers and causal genes is weak.
GAPIT's compressed MLM handles >1 million SNPs in 10,000 individuals; TASSEL fits MLM for structure; PLINK uses standard regression.
SVs are often in weak LD with nearby SNPs; adding causal SVs from a graph pan-genome raised estimated heritability by 24% in tomato.
The 1.5-LOD drop interval is commonly used as an approximate 95% confidence interval for QTL position.
Empirical LOD thresholds come from permutation tests (e.g. 5,000 permutations); with sparse maps Bonferroni is not over-conservative and permutations may be skipped.
Two-dimensional (epistasis) scans need much higher thresholds than 1-D scans (one example: LOD 4.2-4.5 vs 2.5-2.7).

guidance: RILs give more power through homozygosity and replicable genotypes but cannot estimate dominance effects.
Estimated QTL effects are inflated when samples are small (often < 500), true effects are small, and thresholds are stringent; large effects or very large samples make this negligible.

guidance: Around 200 F2 individuals are typically required for map construction and QTL mapping; DH and RIL populations need fewer.
QTL detection power changes little once marker spacing is below ~10 cM; 1-cM maps showed no advantage over low-density maps in a maize study.
In an F2 of 300, the 95% CI of a QTL is > 30 cM and hard to reduce below 10 cM even for strong QTL; biparental intervals are typically 10-30 cM.
Variance explained by detected QTL is overestimated in small populations and close to the true value near n = 1,000.
Simple interval mapping beats single-marker analysis; ICIM keeps CIM's advantages while avoiding its sampling variance.
QTL repeatedly detected across environments using BLUP values are treated as major/stable QTL; G×E and G×G affect mapping accuracy.
Low-depth (1×) sequencing with imputation reduced missing SNP data from 60% to 3% in rice.
A LOD of 3 is the most common fixed threshold for declaring a putative QTL.
source: Rani et al., book chapter (QTL marker technology)
flag: Convention; permutation thresholds preferred where feasible (Xu 2026)

guidance: QTLs are commonly declared significant above LOD 3.0.
Composite interval mapping needs a linkage map first, depends on background-marker choice, and permutations are slow.
source: Rani et al., book chapter (QTL marker technology)

guidance: Loci explaining > 10% of phenotypic variance (PVE) are commonly classed as major QTL.
Meta-QTL analysis needs a high-density consensus map and many QTL for the same trait from different populations and environments.
source: Kaur et al. 2023, Tropical Plant Biology

guidance: BioMercator v4 is the standard tool for QTL meta-analysis and projection onto consensus maps.
source: Sharma et al. 2023, Theor Appl Genet

guidance: Prediction accuracy depends on training-set size, diversity, its relatedness to the breeding set, and phenotype quality; optimize the training set first.
When the training set is less related to the breeding set, it must be larger; accuracy dropped 42% moving from full-sib to half-sib DH maize families.
Including 50-85% of the candidate population typically keeps the accuracy loss below 5%; A-opt and CDmean are suited criteria for choosing which lines.
For low-heritability traits, increase training-set size: power scales with N×h^2.
Marker number needed depends on genome size, LD and trait complexity; complex traits in large low-LD genomes need dense markers; highly heritable oligogenic traits need fewer.
Fitting significant GWAS markers as fixed effects or using the top 100-10,000 markers improved accuracy in several studies.
No single model wins across traits (no free lunch); compare models by cross-validation.
Models are fit on summarized phenotypes or per environment; multi-environment models suit positively correlated environments.
An optimal GS trial chooses which candidates to field-test, distributes them across locations, and plans their layout within fields.

guidance: GBLUP is the common default in plant breeding and is cheaper to compute than Bayesian models; Bayesian models did better for distantly related populations.
SNPs needed 2-3 times the density of microsatellites for comparable accuracy in one study.
High-quality SNPs with MAF > 0.1 are recommended for accuracy; higher marker density and larger training sets improve accuracy; Bayesian MCMC methods can converge slowly.
source: Altaf et al. 2024, Turkish J Botany

guidance: GS within environments outperformed across environments in a chickpea study (320 lines); G×E-aware multi-trait models helped low-heritability lentil traits.
source: Altaf et al. 2024, Turkish J Botany

guidance: Published plant GS studies used roughly 100-4,700 lines and a few hundred to ~270,000 markers.
source: Altaf et al. 2024, Turkish J Botany

guidance: Marker × environmental-covariate models raised accuracy by 17-34%; in maize (2,724 hybrids, 58 environments) GCA/SCA × environment terms added 12-22%.
Machine-learning models sometimes beat GBLUP/Bayesian models, but gains depend on trait architecture and shrink when G×E is modelled.
Multi-trait models strongly improve prediction of a low-heritability trait when it is at least moderately correlated with a high-heritability trait.
Training data need careful experimental design, adequate biological replicates, and recorded environmental heterogeneity within and across sites.
If no repeatable G×E pattern exists, treat the target region as one mega-environment and handle G×E by adequate testing.
Genomic prediction beat pedigree BLUP in aquaculture, with gains reported from a few percent up to ~76%; cross-validation is the usual accuracy check.
source: Yáñez et al. 2023, Reviews in Aquaculture

guidance: Bayesian models (BayesB/BayesC) did better for moderate-to-large-effect QTL; GBLUP suits polygenic traits.
source: Yáñez et al. 2023, Reviews in Aquaculture

guidance: Imputed low-density panels lost only ~3% accuracy versus full genotypes; GWAS-prioritized SNPs added 1.2-13.3% accuracy.
source: Yáñez et al. 2023, Reviews in Aquaculture

guidance: Imputing missing genotypes improved predictive ability by 5-18%; BayesR marginally beat GBLUP for disease traits.
Disease resistance traits often have low heritability (~10% for WSSV in grow-out shrimp); evaluate resistance under relevant environments.
Cattle fertility traits had heritabilities of about 0.10-0.18.
Low-quality cells have few detected genes, low counts and a high mitochondrial fraction; filter by manual thresholds or sample-wise MAD-based automatic thresholds.
source: Heumos et al. 2023, Nat Rev Genet

guidance: Mitochondrial thresholds depend on tissue: ~30% mitochondrial mRNA is normal in heart cells but ≤5% in low-energy tissues. Example published filters: 200-6,000 genes, >200 UMIs, <10% mito.
High-throughput runs can have up to ~40% doublet barcodes; count/gene filters alone don't remove them, so use a doublet detector.
source: Su et al. 2022, Military Medical Research

guidance: Recent benchmarks favour scDblFinder for accuracy and speed.
source: Heumos et al. 2023, Nat Rev Genet

guidance: A benchmark recommended DoubletFinder for detection accuracy and downstream performance.

guidance: Bulk scaling methods (TPM, upper quartile, TMM, DESeq) are not appropriate for scRNA-seq; scran pooling performed best in simulations; values are usually log(x+1) transformed after scaling.
source: Su et al. 2022, Military Medical Research

guidance: Choose normalization based on the downstream analysis; correcting one biological effect can hide another.
source: Heumos et al. 2023, Nat Rev Genet

guidance: For complex integrations (atlases) deep-learning methods (scVI, scANVI, scGen) or Scanorama performed best; for simpler tasks Harmony is preferred.
source: Heumos et al. 2023, Nat Rev Genet

guidance: Harmony is fastest; Seurat CCA mixes batches moderately; LIGER mixes most strongly, sometimes at the cost of cell-type purity.
source: Su et al. 2022, Military Medical Research

guidance: MNN/fastMNN batch correction can inflate false discoveries in downstream DE; avoid DE on batch-corrected values.
Use Leiden clustering at several resolutions; don't draw conclusions from 2-D embeddings alone.
source: Heumos et al. 2023, Nat Rev Genet

guidance: Two or three PCs suffice for visualization, but several to dozens are kept for clustering and trajectories.
source: Su et al. 2022, Military Medical Research

guidance: Testing cells as independent replicates (pseudoreplication) inflates FDR. Aggregate to pseudobulk per sample and use limma/edgeR/DESeq2, or mixed models; avoid naive per-cell Wilcoxon tests.
source: Heumos et al. 2023, Nat Rev Genet

guidance: Pseudobulk approaches such as edgeR-LRT and DESeq2-Wald are recommended for DE.
UMI data (10x, Drop-seq) are fit by non-zero-inflated Poisson/NB for almost all genes; about half the genes in non-UMI Smart-seq2 data favour zero-inflated models.

guidance: With UMI counts, zero-inflated models are not needed; spatial transcriptomics also doesn't need zero inflation.
For UMI data, observed counts gave the best clustering; imputation mainly helps non-UMI data and can be skipped when depth is adequate.
Score clustering with the adjusted Rand index and DE with F1 at 5% FDR against known truth.

guidance: ARI and NMI assess clustering against labels; silhouette and Dunn index assess cluster separation.
CellRanger took ~22 h and up to 30 GB RAM for 784M reads (~50,000 cells at 15,000 reads/cell); ≥32 threads and 128 GB RAM recommended.
High clustering scores don't guarantee correct cell types; resolution and cell-type number are often subjective choices.

This review reports specific figures (Leiden ARI 0.85-0.92; Harmony ~30% faster than BBKNN; SCTransform handles zero-inflation better than scran; GLM-PCA ~20% fewer false positives than MAST) without clear dataset context.

guidance: Only 1-10% of peaks are detected per cell in scATAC data; rare cell types may lack enough cells for peak calling.
source: Heumos et al. 2023, Nat Rev Genet

guidance: Bulk benchmarks suggest edgeR for small sample sizes and DESeq2 for large ones; remove low-count, low-TSS-enrichment cell clusters.
source: Heumos et al. 2023, Nat Rev Genet

guidance: Target about 10 million read pairs for standard high-depth ATAC libraries; nucleosome-positioning studies need ~150-200 million reads (human).
36 bp reads are sufficient for most applications; reads over 100 bp add little because most fragments are <200 bp.
Prefer biological over technical replicates when resources are limited; merge technical replicates at the peak-merging step.
TSS enrichment scores depend on the TSS set used, so they aren't comparable across tools or species; use each pipeline's pass thresholds.
Well-amplified libraries typically have <10% duplicate reads, but this depends on depth and isn't used alone to judge quality.
Run a low-depth sequencing check of sample quality before deep sequencing.
Call peaks per sample, then merge into a union peak set using iterative overlap with fixed-width (501 bp) peaks, avoiding bias toward deeper libraries.
Normalize using reads in TSS regions (invariant across samples) rather than reads in peaks, which must be recomputed whenever the peak set changes.
DESeq/DESeq2 minimize false positives; edgeR or limma give higher sensitivity, with limma best for low-signal regions such as distal enhancers.
Correct for the Tn5 offset and insertion bias before TF footprinting.
About 10× WGS gave >99% genome coverage with accurate variant calls in pigs; below 4× false-positive variants rise and coverage falls to ~95%.
source: Lu et al. 2025, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Low-coverage resequencing (<1×) suits large population studies; Pool-seq is cheap but cannot give haplotypes or LD.
source: Lu et al. 2025, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Nanopore at ~10× found 27% more novel SVs than short-read NGS in a human population study.
source: Lu et al. 2025, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Depth (×) is total sequenced bases over genome size; coverage is the fraction of the genome read at least once.
source: Lu et al. 2025, Int J Mol Sci

guidance: Nanopore error can reach ~15% in low-complexity sequence.
Targeted sequencing can reach ~5,000× depth for rare alleles or low-frequency clones.
PacBio HiFi/CCS reaches up to ~99.95% accuracy; ONT R10 chemistry >99%; after base-calling, typical error is ~1% (PacBio) and ~5% (ONT); raw PacBio CLR error is ~10-15% and random.

guidance: PacBio HiFi reads are ~99.8% accurate at ~13.5 kb average; Nanopore reads average >20 kb (max >2 Mb) at ~90% base accuracy.

guidance: Assembly-based variant calling identifies SVs in complex regions more accurately than mapping short reads to one reference.

PacBio HiFi or Nanopore ultra-long reads are highly recommended for pan-genome assemblies; HiFi alone can complete T2T assemblies of small genomes like Arabidopsis and rice; HiFi is used to polish ONT assemblies.
Graph genomes align short reads better in regions with complex SVs (tools: vg, Giraffe).
Typical shotgun metagenomes use 20-60 million reads; ~0.5 million may suffice for taxonomic profiling only; ultra-deep sequencing is needed to recover genomes of novel species.
Assembly-based strain haplotyping needs high coverage (~100× recommended for BHap); genome-wide variant methods need more coverage than local methods.
edgeR or DESeq2 can be used for differential expression on metatranscriptomic gene counts.
Amplicon reads are traditionally clustered into OTUs at 97% similarity.
Several genomic language models did not outperform non-gLM baselines on human prediction tasks; evaluate against simple baselines.
Only ~3.3% of the human genome appears constrained and ~50% is repetitive; repeats should be downweighted or downsampled in gLM training.

A. thaliana self-fertilizes ~97% of the time; its structure is continuous isolation by distance at every scale, with little continental structure and no natural population breaks (5,707 plants, 149 SNPs).
flag: simitall's synthetic Arabidopsis panel uses discrete subpopulations; this is a simplification of continuous isolation by distance

guidance: In inbred panels (mouse strains, maize, Arabidopsis), complex structure inflates false positives that genomic control or structured association cannot fix; mixed models with kinship (EMMA) correct it.
GEMMA fits the exact mixed model about n times faster than EMMA (n = sample size), making exact genome-wide LMM practical for large samples.
MLM with structure (Q) and kinship (K) controls false positives but also removes true positives; Q and Q+K models still beat naive single-marker tests.
FarmCPU alternates a fixed-effect model (associated markers as covariates) and a random-effect model; it controls false positives as well as MLM with fewer false negatives and less computing time.

guidance: The rMVP authors recommend including the top 3-5 PCs as covariates to control false positives from population structure.

guidance: DESeq2 shrinks dispersion and log fold-change estimates for stability with few replicates; genes of similar mean are assumed to have similar dispersion, and shrinkage weakens as sample size grows.
Raw fold changes are noisy for low-count genes; rank genes by shrunken log fold changes rather than raw ones.

sctransform uses Pearson residuals from regularized negative-binomial regression with cell depth as a covariate; an unconstrained NB overfits, so parameters are pooled across genes of similar abundance. No pseudocount or log transform is needed. For UMI data only.

In a simulated 1,000 cM genome with 1-cM markers, prediction accuracy was 0.32 when only the largest effects were fitted by least squares (and they were overestimated), 0.73 with BLUP, and 0.85 with Bayesian priors even when the prior was wrong.
